events.title: Dot-com melt-up: Nasdaq nearly doubles in 1999
events.summary: Capital poured into internet, telecom-equipment and software names in the final leg of the dot-com bubble. The Nasdaq Composite rose 85.6% in 1999 against a 21.0% total return for the S&P 500, and the index peaked at a 5,048.62 close on 10 March 2000 (5,132.52 intraday). The Fed was tightening into the top, raising rates again on 21 March 2000.
events.evidence: Nasdaq Composite 1999 calendar-year return +85.59%; record close 5,048.62 on 2000-03-10.

events.title: Dot-com bust: tech falls 82% peak-to-trough
events.summary: The Nasdaq fell roughly 78% from its March 2000 peak to October 2002, with the S&P 500 technology sector down 82.4% and telecom down 74.1% between 24 March 2000 and 9 October 2002 versus 49.2% for the S&P 500. Cisco, briefly the world's most valuable company at over $500 billion in late March 2000, lost about 80% of its value. The Fed began an emergency easing cycle with a 50 bp cut to 6% on 3 January 2001, but capital kept leaving tech for staples (+24% over the bear) and value.
events.evidence: S&P 500 Information Technology sector -82.37% from 2000-03-24 to 2002-10-09 vs S&P 500 -49.15%.

events.title: 2003 reflation: Nasdaq +50% on 1% Fed funds
events.summary: With the fed funds rate at a four-decade low of 1% (the Fed only began raising it, to 1.25%, on 30 June 2004), beaten-down tech led the recovery. The Nasdaq Composite gained 50.0% in 2003 versus 28.7% for the S&P 500, the first year of a new cycle after three consecutive losing years (-39.3%, -21.1%, -31.5%).
events.evidence: Nasdaq Composite 2003 return +50.01% vs S&P 500 total return +28.68%.

events.title: Measured-pace hiking cycle: tech lags energy and value
events.summary: The Fed raised rates 17 times from 1% to 5.25% between June 2004 and June 2006, and leadership passed to energy, materials, homebuilders and financials. The Nasdaq returned 8.6% in 2004, 1.4% in 2005 and 9.5% in 2006 against S&P 500 total returns of 10.9%, 4.9% and 15.8%, a persistent relative drag for growth-heavy tech during the commodity and credit boom.
events.evidence: Fed funds target raised to 1.25% on 2004-06-30 and to 5.25% on 2006-06-29; Nasdaq 2005 return +1.37% vs S&P 500 +4.91%.

events.title: Google buys YouTube for $1.65 billion
events.summary: Google agreed on 9 October 2006 to acquire YouTube for $1.65 billion in stock, closing 13 November 2006. The deal marked the start of the shift of video advertising dollars from traditional media toward internet platforms, a theme that would weigh on legacy media valuations for the next two decades. YouTube was already serving roughly 100 million video views per day by mid-2006.
events.evidence: Acquisition announced 2006-10-09 for $1.65 billion in Google stock; closed 2006-11-13.

events.title: iPhone launch starts the smartphone supercycle
events.summary: The iPhone went on sale on 29 June 2007 and Apple's shares rose from roughly $77 at the end of 2006 to about $200 by December 2007, a gain of around 160% in a year when the S&P 500 returned 5.5% and the Nasdaq 9.8%. The product reshaped the handset, component and wireless-carrier value chain (AT&T's exclusive), and the semiconductor content of phones became a decade-long demand driver.
events.evidence: Apple closed 2007 at about $200.96 versus $76.77 a year earlier (pre-split prices).

sources.title: This Day In Market History: Apple Introduces The iPhone

events.title: Credit crunch: Fed starts cutting, financial earnings collapse
events.summary: The Fed cut 50 bp to 4.75% on 18 September 2007, warning that tightening credit could intensify the housing correction. By 15 February 2008 analysts expected S&P 500 financial-sector profits to fall 23% in Q1 2008 (versus +5% expected the prior October), with mortgage insurers and Countrywide down 35-67% over three months. Capital rotated out of banks and brokers and, by May 2008, technology had overtaken financials as the largest S&P 500 sector.
events.evidence: Thomson Financial consensus on 2008-02-15: Q1 2008 financial-sector earnings -23%; ex-financials S&P 500 earnings +9%.

events.title: Utilities outperform but still fall 46% in the GFC bear
events.summary: Regulated utilities drew defensive flows during the financial crisis yet still lost 45.9% peak-to-trough versus 56.8% for the S&P 500, because credit-spread widening hit their leveraged balance sheets and merchant generators. The 0-0.25% fed funds rate set on 16 December 2008 and the start of asset purchases then turned utilities into the bond proxy of the next decade.

events.title: GFC: tech falls less than the market and becomes the largest sector
events.summary: Technology fell about 43.7% in 2008 (Nasdaq -40.5%) and 53.0% peak-to-trough, less than the S&P 500's 56.8% and far less than financials' 82.6%, because balance sheets were cash-rich and had no credit exposure. In May 2008 tech overtook financials as the largest S&P 500 sector weight, a position it has not relinquished. The relative resilience set up tech's leadership in the 2009-2012 recovery.
events.evidence: S&P 500 Information Technology -52.95% peak-to-trough (2007-10-09 to 2009-03-09) vs Financials -82.62%; Nasdaq 2008 return -40.54%.

events.title: Visa prices the largest US IPO in history mid-crisis
events.summary: Visa raised about $17.9 billion (US$19.1 billion with the overallotment) at $44 a share on 18 March 2008, then the largest IPO in US history, days after Bear Stearns was rescued. The listing created a liquid, asset-light payments bucket inside the IT sector that compounded through the financial crisis while bank balance sheets shrank; Mastercard had listed in 2006.
events.evidence: 406 million shares sold at $44 on 2008-03-18, raising about $17.9 billion.

events.title: Commodity supercycle peak and crash
events.summary: Oil peaked at about $147 a barrel on 11 July 2008 and collapsed to $30.28 by 23 December 2008 as the credit crunch crushed demand expectations; nickel fell from about $51,000 to $11,550 a tonne and the Baltic Dry Index from 11,440 to 715. S&P 500 materials fell 59.6% peak-to-trough versus 56.8% for the index, with miners and chemical producers hit by destocking and the dollar squeeze.
events.evidence: WTI/Brent peak about $147 on 2008-07-11; WTI spot $30.28 on 2008-12-23; Materials sector -59.55% from 2007-10-09 to 2009-03-09.

events.title: Lehman bankruptcy and the financials collapse
events.summary: Lehman Brothers filed the largest bankruptcy in US history on 15 September 2008; the Dow fell 4.4% that day and AIG plunged 61%. S&P 500 financials lost about 57% in calendar 2008 and 82.6% from the 9 October 2007 peak to the 9 March 2009 low, versus 56.8% for the index. The Fed announced $600 billion of agency and MBS purchases on 25 November 2008 and cut to 0-0.25% on 16 December 2008.

events.title: DRAM oversupply bankrupts Qimonda
events.summary: Commodity DRAM prices fell through 2008 on oversupply and Qimonda, Infineon's memory spin-off, filed for insolvency on 23 January 2009 after a German bailout fell apart; its NYSE shares had dropped to $0.05 by November 2008 and it sold its Inotera stake to Micron for about $400 million. The failure removed capacity from a sector that was consolidating toward three DRAM makers, the structure behind later memory price cycles.
events.evidence: Qimonda AG filed for insolvency protection on 2009-01-23; net sales fell to EUR 1.79 billion from EUR 3.61 billion.

events.title: Smartphone and cloud build-out leads the QE recovery
events.summary: With the Fed at zero and buying bonds (QE2 of $600 billion announced 3 November 2010), capital rotated into the mobile and cloud build-out: the Nasdaq returned 43.9% in 2009, 16.9% in 2010 and 15.9% in 2012 versus 26.5%, 15.1% and 16.0% for the S&P 500. Global smartphone shipments reached 725 million units in 2012 and about 1 billion in 2013 (+38%), and Apple set a then-record $624 billion market capitalisation on 20 August 2012.
events.evidence: Apple market capitalisation record of $624 billion on 2012-08-20; smartphone shipments about 1 billion in 2013, up 38% from 725 million in 2012.

events.title: Stress-test results end the bank panic
events.summary: The Fed's Supervisory Capital Assessment Program results on 7 May 2009 found 10 of 19 large firms needed about $74.6 billion of capital (Bank of America $33.9 billion), a credible number that let banks raise equity and unlocked the rally in financials from the 9 March 2009 low. Combined with QE1 purchases, the result pulled capital back into banks and brokers through 2009, although the sector never regained its pre-crisis index weight.
events.evidence: SCAP results released 2009-05-07: 10 of 19 banks required additional capital totalling about $74.6 billion.

events.title: Comcast agrees to buy control of NBC Universal
events.summary: On 3 December 2009 Comcast and GE announced a deal valuing NBC Universal at $30 billion, with Comcast taking 51% (closed 28 January 2011) and buying the rest in March 2013. The transaction fused cable distribution with content, a vertical-integration template later followed by AT&T-Time Warner, and it marked GE's retreat from media during the recession.
events.evidence: Deal announced 2009-12-03 valuing NBC Universal at $30 billion; majority stake closed 2011-01-28.

events.title: Dodd-Frank signed: Volcker Rule, Durbin and the CFPB
events.summary: President Obama signed Dodd-Frank on 21 July 2010, introducing the Volcker Rule limits on proprietary trading, the Durbin amendment capping debit interchange, the CFPB and systemic-risk designations. Higher capital and compliance costs capped bank returns on equity for most of the decade and pushed activity toward non-bank lenders and payment networks; the law was partially rolled back in May 2018.
events.evidence: Dodd-Frank Act signed into law on 2010-07-21.

events.title: Utilities best sector of 2011 as yields collapse
events.summary: As the Eurozone crisis and the US downgrade drove Treasury yields to record lows and the Fed extended its zero-rate guidance, utilities returned 19.9% in 2011, the best S&P 500 sector against a 2.1% index return and -17.1% for financials. The year established the 'bond proxy' rotation pattern: utilities, staples and telecom absorb capital whenever real yields fall and growth fears rise.
events.evidence: S&P 500 Utilities 2011 total return +19.9% (best sector) vs S&P 500 +2.1%.

events.title: Copper tops $10,000 and the commodity supercycle peaks
events.summary: Copper rose above $10,000 a tonne in early 2011 and silver hit $47.94 on 29 April 2011 on China's post-stimulus demand, but 2011 marked the top of the supercycle: silver fell 12% on 2 May, and by 2013 copper was down about 33% and iron ore 36% from the early-2011 peaks. S&P 500 materials returned -9.6% in 2011 against +2.1% for the index as capital left cyclicals for bond proxies.
events.evidence: Copper exceeded $10,000 per tonne in early 2011; S&P 500 Materials 2011 return -9.6% vs S&P 500 +2.1%.

events.title: Fukushima halves uranium prices and starts a decade-long nuclear bear market
events.summary: The 11 March 2011 Fukushima accident led to reactor shutdowns in Japan and Germany's exit decision; uranium spot prices fell by more than 50% from pre-accident levels and producers cut capacity, closed operations and deferred projects for years. The uranium ETF (URA, launched November 2010) and Cameco spent most of the following decade in drawdown, the base from which the 2023-2025 'nuclear renaissance' re-rating started.
events.evidence: Uranium spot price fell more than 50% after the March 2011 Fukushima disaster, with producers cutting capacity.

events.title: US downgrade and Eurozone crisis: financials worst sector of 2011
events.summary: S&P stripped the US of its AAA rating on 6 August 2011 and the S&P 500 fell 6.7% on 8 August, with about $2.5 trillion of global equity value erased in a day as the Eurozone crisis spread to Italy and Spain; European regulators banned short selling of banks on 11 August. S&P 500 financials finished 2011 down 17.1%, the worst sector, versus +2.1% for the index, while utilities led at +19.9%.
events.evidence: S&P 500 -6.7% on 2011-08-08; Financials sector 2011 return -17.1% vs S&P 500 +2.1%.

events.title: Facebook IPO at $38 breaks, halves by September
events.summary: Facebook priced the largest internet IPO at $38 on 18 May 2012, fell below the offer price on day two and bottomed near $17.73 in early September 2012 amid doubts about mobile monetisation. The flop chilled consumer-internet listings for a year, yet marked the arrival of social media as an index-scale ad platform that would be reclassified into Communication Services in 2018.
events.evidence: IPO priced at $38 on 2012-05-18; shares traded below $18 in September 2012, less than half the offer price.

events.title: QE3 and housing recovery make financials the best sector of 2012
events.summary: The Fed launched open-ended purchases of $40 billion a month of agency MBS on 13 September 2012 and extended zero-rate guidance to mid-2015, supporting mortgage credit and bank balance sheets. S&P 500 financials returned 28.8% in 2012, the best sector against 16.0% for the index, as the Eurozone tail risk faded after the ECB's 'whatever it takes' pledge.
events.evidence: S&P 500 Financials 2012 total return +28.8% vs S&P 500 +16.0%; QE3 announced 2012-09-13.

events.title: Dell goes private in a $24.4 billion LBO as PCs shrink
events.summary: Michael Dell and Silver Lake announced a $24.4 billion leveraged buyout on 5 February 2013 (closed 30 October 2013 at $13.88 a share) as PC demand fell under tablets and smartphones. The deal removed a major hardware name from public markets and symbolised capital leaving legacy PC and server hardware for mobile and cloud; Dell relisted in 2018 as an AI-server play.
events.evidence: LBO announced 2013-02-05 for $24.4 billion; completed 2013-10-30.

events.title: Taper tantrum hits utilities, REITs and telecom
events.summary: Ben Bernanke's 22 May 2013 remarks on reducing bond purchases sent 10-year yields sharply higher and triggered a rotation out of bond proxies: in the week of 20 May utilities fell 3.4% and REITs 4.4% against a 1.07% drop in the S&P 500, with reported drawdowns of about 9% for XLU and 12% for VNQ over the episode. Utilities finished 2013 up 13.2% against 32.4% for the index, and the Fed began tapering on 18 December 2013.
events.evidence: Week of 2013-05-20: Utilities -3.4%, REITs -4.4%, S&P 500 -1.07%; Utilities 2013 return +13.2% vs S&P 500 +32.4%.

events.title: Telecom lags as taper talk lifts yields
events.summary: High-dividend telecom carriers traded as bond proxies alongside utilities and REITs and were sold once the Fed signalled tapering in May 2013. S&P 500 telecom services returned 11.5% in 2013, the second-worst sector, against 32.4% for the S&P 500 and 28.4% for technology, as capital rotated from yield toward growth and cyclicals.
events.evidence: S&P 500 Telecom Services 2013 total return +11.5% vs S&P 500 +32.4%.

events.title: Utilities return 29% in 2014 as yields fall again
events.summary: Contrary to consensus for higher rates, the 10-year yield fell through 2014 as the Fed completed tapering and global growth disappointed, and utilities returned 29.0%, the second-best S&P 500 sector after real estate against a 13.7% index return. Energy (-7.8%) was the worst sector as the oil crash began, the first leg of the 2014-2016 industrial recession.
events.evidence: S&P 500 Utilities 2014 total return +29.0% vs S&P 500 +13.7%; Energy -7.8%.

events.title: Sony Pictures hack puts cybersecurity on the map as a theme
events.summary: The Guardians of Peace leak of Sony Pictures data on 24 November 2014, formally attributed by the FBI to North Korea on 19 December, made breach risk a board-level issue two weeks after the first cybersecurity ETF (HACK) launched on 11 November 2014. Security budgets became a non-discretionary line in enterprise IT spending, the foundation of the sector's later premium valuation.
events.evidence: Sony Pictures data leaked 2014-11-24; FBI linked the attack to North Korea on 2014-12-19.

events.title: Avago-Broadcom and the 2015 semiconductor M&A wave
events.summary: Avago agreed to buy Broadcom for about $37 billion on 28 May 2015 (closed January 2016), days before Intel's $16.7 billion Altera deal, after NXP's $11.8 billion Freescale purchase in March. Announced semiconductor acquisitions totalled $72.6 billion in the first half of 2015 alone, nearly six times the prior five-year annual average, as slowing unit growth pushed the industry toward scale and pricing power that underpinned its later margin expansion.
events.evidence: IC Insights: H1 2015 announced semiconductor M&A of $72.6 billion, about 6x the prior five-year annual average; Avago-Broadcom valued at about $37 billion.

events.title: China devaluation, oil below $30 and the Glencore scare
events.summary: China devalued the yuan on 11 August 2015 and global markets fell on 24 August; Glencore, carrying about $30 billion of debt, posted a $676 million first-half operating loss and its shares crashed on 28 September 2015. Oil fell below $30 on 3 February 2016, down almost 75% from mid-2014. S&P 500 materials returned -8.4% and energy -21.1% in 2015 versus +1.4% for the index, even as the Fed lifted rates off zero on 16 December 2015.
events.evidence: Oil below $30 on 2016-02-03, down almost 75% from mid-2014; Materials 2015 return -8.4%, Energy -21.1% vs S&P 500 +1.4%.

events.title: 2016 reflation: materials and energy lead off the February low
events.summary: From the February 2016 commodity low, a weaker dollar, Chinese stimulus and then the November election's infrastructure and tariff expectations pulled capital back into cyclicals. S&P 500 materials returned 16.7% and energy 27.4% in 2016 versus 12.0% for the index, with steel and copper producers among the strongest groups; US indices set records in July 2016 after the Brexit dip.
events.evidence: S&P 500 Materials 2016 total return +16.7%, Energy +27.4% (best sector) vs S&P 500 +12.0%.

events.title: Trump election: banks post best month on record
events.summary: The 8 November 2016 election triggered a rotation into banks on expectations of deregulation, tax cuts and higher rates: the SPDR S&P Bank ETF (KBE) rose 18.69% in November 2016, its best month on record, against 3.42% for the S&P 500, with Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley up about 23% and the 10-year yield rising from roughly 1.8% to 2.4%. The KBW bank index had gained nearly 14% within a week of the vote. Regional banks were up 27% by early February 2017 when Trump signed executive actions to begin unwinding Dodd-Frank.

events.title: Tech lags the post-election rotation into banks and industrials
events.summary: In the week after the 2016 election Apple and other large technology names fell while banks and industrials surged, on concern that trade and tax policy would hurt overseas sales and because investors funded the cyclical rotation by selling crowded growth. Technology finished 2016 up 13.9%, roughly in line with the index (12.0%) but well behind financials (22.8%) and energy (27.4%); the lag reversed into the 2017 melt-up.
events.evidence: Reuters, 2016-11-10: banks and industrials surged while Apple and other tech shares fell; Technology 2016 return +13.9% vs Financials +22.8%.

events.title: 2017 synchronized growth: tech returns 39%, FAANG 46%
events.summary: Global synchronized growth, low volatility and the December 2017 tax cut drove a melt-up in large-cap technology: the S&P 500 IT sector returned 38.8% in 2017 against 21.8% for the index, and Goldman Sachs put the FAANG group at +46.5%. Telecom (-1.3%) and energy (-1.0%) were the only negative sectors, the mirror image of the 2016 rotation. Reuters noted the sector traded at 19x forward earnings versus 18x for the index, a modest premium by later standards.

events.title: Equifax breach: 147.9 million records and a $575 million settlement
events.summary: Equifax disclosed on 7 September 2017 that attackers had accessed data on about 147.9 million Americans; its shares fell about 13% the next day and the company agreed a roughly $575 million settlement in July 2019. Together with WannaCry earlier that year, the breach pushed security spending up the enterprise priority list and supported the re-rating of cybersecurity vendors relative to broader software.
events.evidence: Equifax shares fell about 13% on 2017-09-08; July 2019 settlement of about $575 million.

events.title: Section 232 steel and aluminum tariffs and the start of the trade war
events.summary: Trump announced 25% steel and 10% aluminum tariffs on 1 March 2018 and signed the order on 8 March; on 22 March he directed Section 301 tariffs on about $50 billion of Chinese goods and the Dow fell 724 points (2.9%). Domestic steelmakers initially benefited, but the broader materials sector returned -14.7% in 2018 against -4.4% for the S&P 500 as global growth and Chinese demand expectations weakened.
events.evidence: Section 232 order signed 2018-03-08 (25% steel, 10% aluminum); S&P 500 Materials 2018 return -14.7% vs S&P 500 -4.4%.

events.title: Dodd-Frank rollback raises the SIFI threshold to $250 billion
events.summary: The Economic Growth, Regulatory Relief and Consumer Protection Act, signed 24 May 2018, lifted the enhanced-supervision threshold from $50 billion to $250 billion of assets, exempted banks under $10 billion from the Volcker Rule and cut stress-test frequency for mid-sized banks. It was the regulatory payoff of the 2016 bank rally, although the relief later drew blame after Silicon Valley Bank, whose CEO had lobbied for the law, failed in 2023.
events.evidence: Act signed 2018-05-24; SIFI threshold raised from $50 billion to $250 billion in assets.

events.title: Facebook loses $119 billion in a day on slowing growth
events.summary: After the Cambridge Analytica revelations of 17 March 2018 had already knocked about 24% ($134 billion) off the stock by 26 March, Facebook's 25 July 2018 guidance for slowing revenue growth and higher costs erased over $119 billion of market value on 26 July, then the largest one-day loss for any US company. The episode introduced regulatory and privacy risk into platform valuations just before the sector's September 2018 reclassification.
events.evidence: Over $119 billion wiped off Facebook's market capitalisation on 2018-07-26 after a growth warning.

events.title: GICS creates Communication Services: Alphabet, Facebook, Netflix leave tech and discretionary
events.summary: S&P Dow Jones Indices and MSCI, in a change announced 11 January 2018 and implemented after the close on 28 September 2018, renamed Telecommunication Services as Communication Services and moved Alphabet and Facebook out of Information Technology and Netflix and Comcast out of Consumer Discretionary. About 23 S&P 500 companies and roughly 10% of index market cap changed sector, forcing sector-ETF rebalancing (XLK lost Alphabet and Facebook) and turning a 2% bond-proxy telecom sector into a 10% growth sector.
events.evidence: Changes effective after the close on 2018-09-28; Lipper estimated 23 S&P 500 companies and roughly 10% of index market cap reclassified.

events.title: Q4 2018 selloff: Fed hikes, trade war and Apple's December-quarter slump
events.summary: The Nasdaq fell 17.5% and the S&P 500 13.97% in Q4 2018 as the Fed hiked a fourth time on 19 December to 2.25-2.5% and US-China trade talks stalled; the Dow and S&P posted their worst December since 1931 and the Nasdaq 100 entered a bear market on 21 December. Apple fell more than 31% in the December quarter ahead of its January 2019 China revenue warning, and semiconductors led the decline. Technology still finished 2018 at -0.3% versus -4.4% for the index.

events.title: PG&E collapses on Camp Fire liabilities and files Chapter 11
events.summary: PG&E shares fell 60% between the day before the 8 November 2018 Camp Fire and 7 January 2019, then dropped 52% to $8.38 on 14 January 2019 when the company said it would file for Chapter 11 (filed 29 January) facing at least $30 billion of wildfire liabilities. The bankruptcy introduced wildfire liability as a structural discount for Western utilities and reshaped how investors price inverse condemnation risk; PG&E emerged on 1 July 2020.

events.title: Huawei entity listing hits semiconductors
events.summary: On 15 May 2019 Trump declared a national emergency over threats to US technology and Commerce added Huawei to the Entity List, cutting off a customer worth 13% of Micron's sales and about 10% for Skyworks and Qorvo; Micron fell 11.4% between 3 and 15 May and the Philadelphia semiconductor index's May decline reached about 14%, after tariffs on $200 billion of Chinese goods had been raised to 25% on 10 May. The G20 truce on 29 June and the Fed's July pivot reversed the move, and semiconductors led the market for the rest of 2019.
events.evidence: Micron -11.4% from 2019-05-03 to 2019-05-15 with 13% of sales from Huawei; Philadelphia semiconductor index down about 14% in May 2019.

events.title: Fed pivot: technology returns 50% in 2019
events.summary: After the December 2018 hike, the Fed reversed course, cutting 25 bp to 2-2.25% on 31 July 2019 (the first of three cuts) and ending balance-sheet runoff early. Falling discount rates and the Phase One trade truce, signed 15 January 2020, drove the S&P 500 IT sector to a 50.3% return in 2019, the best sector against 31.5% for the index, with semiconductors and Apple leading and multiple expansion doing most of the work.
events.evidence: FOMC cut to 2-2.25% on 2019-07-31; S&P 500 Information Technology 2019 total return +50.3% vs S&P 500 +31.5%.

events.title: Disney+ launches with 10 million day-one sign-ups
events.summary: Disney+ launched on 12 November 2019 and reported more than 10 million sign-ups on day one, reaching 86.8 million subscribers by 10 December 2020. The launch validated the streaming pivot for legacy media and briefly re-rated Disney and peers as growth stocks, even as cord-cutting accelerated (MoffettNathanson called Q1 2019 the worst quarter ever for pay-TV losses) and set up the 2022 streaming-profitability reckoning.
events.evidence: More than 10 million Disney+ sign-ups within the first day (2019-11-12); 86.8 million subscribers announced 2020-12-10.

events.title: COVID crash and the work-from-home boom
events.summary: The Dow fell 12.93% on 16 March 2020 after the Fed's emergency cut to 0-0.25% and $700 billion of purchases on 15 March, but the pandemic then pulled capital into digital winners: Zoom was up about 580% year-to-date by November 2020, global PC demand rose about 13%, Apple became the first $2 trillion company on 19 August 2020, and the Nasdaq returned 43.6% for the year. S&P 500 technology returned 43.9% against 18.4% for the index while energy lost 33.7%.
events.evidence: S&P 500 Information Technology 2020 total return +43.9% vs S&P 500 +18.4%; Nasdaq Composite 2020 +43.64%.

events.title: T-Mobile completes the Sprint merger
events.summary: T-Mobile closed its acquisition of Sprint on 1 April 2020, consolidating the US wireless market to three national carriers and giving T-Mobile the mid-band spectrum that underpinned its 5G share gains. The consolidation improved pricing discipline for the carriers and later drove Verizon and AT&T into fiber and spectrum acquisitions to keep pace.
events.evidence: Sprint became a T-Mobile US subsidiary on 2020-04-01; the Sprint brand was retired 2020-08-02.

events.title: Fed caps bank dividends and bars buybacks after COVID stress scenarios
events.summary: On 25 June 2020 the Fed published stress results with pandemic sensitivity scenarios projecting $560-700 billion of loan losses across 34 banks, barred share repurchases and capped dividends at Q2 levels for the third quarter. With rates at zero flattening the curve, financials returned -1.7% in 2020 against +18.4% for the S&P 500, their worst relative year since 2011, before the vaccine and reflation trade reversed the gap in 2021.

The Semiconductor Industry Association's May 2025 comments argued for exemptions for firms investing in US fabs, the structure adopted in the January 2026 proclamation, and chipmakers with US fab pledges (TSMC, Micron, Apple's suppliers) traded on expected offsets.
events.evidence: Section 232 investigation into semiconductor and equipment imports directed in April 2025 (Bloomberg, 2025-04-14); SIA comments filed May 2025.

events.title: Charter-Cox and AT&T-Lumen: cable and fiber consolidate
events.summary: Charter announced a merger with Cox Communications on 16 May 2025 (Cox Enterprises taking 23% of the combined company; closed 20 August 2026) and AT&T agreed on 21 May 2025 to buy Lumen's mass-market fiber business for $5.75 billion (closed 2 February 2026). events.title: Trump's nuclear executive orders target 10 new large reactors by 2030

Oklo was selected for DOE's Reactor Pilot Program that month, and the orders extended the 2024 hyperscaler-driven re-rating of uranium, fuel-cycle and SMR names.

Domestic steelmakers gained pricing power while metal-consuming manufacturers and chemical producers absorbed higher input costs; materials returned 10.5% in 2025 against 17.9% for the S&P 500.

events.title: Fed proposes and finalises the enhanced supplementary leverage ratio cut
events.summary: On 25 June 2025 the Fed voted 5-2 to propose recalibrating the enhanced supplementary leverage ratio for the eight US GSIBs; dissenting Governor Barr estimated it would cut tier 1 capital requirements at their bank subsidiaries by 27%, or $210 billion. The rule was finalised on 25 November 2025 with the bank-level buffer capped at 1 percentage point, the first major post-crisis capital rollback and the centrepiece of the 2025 bank-deregulation trade; Basel III endgame was re-proposed with reductions on 19 March 2026.

events.title: One Big Beautiful Bill Act: solar and wind credits phased out, nuclear and manufacturing kept
events.summary: Signed 4 July 2025, the OBBBA ends wind and solar credits for projects not started by June 2026 or online by December 2027, ends residential clean-energy and EV credits after 2025, but keeps advanced-manufacturing (45X), carbon-capture and nuclear credits and adds a 10% nuclear bonus, alongside permanent 100% expensing and a new factory-depreciation allowance. The law split the reshoring theme: solar and residential-energy names derated while nuclear, factory construction and electrical-equipment beneficiaries kept their policy tailwind.

US producers (Freeport) and recyclers benefited from the arbitrage while wire, cable and electrical-equipment makers faced higher costs for the grid and data-center build-out.

A federal judge ruled the fee unlawful on 8 June 2026, but DHS proposed a $103,265 fee by rule in August 2026, keeping labor-cost and delivery-model risk on Cognizant, Infosys and peers. An employee share sale valued OpenAI at $500 billion. events.title: Supreme Court strikes down IEEPA tariffs; Section 122 and 301 duties replace them
events.summary: In Learning Resources v. The administration replaced them with a 10%, then 15%, Section 122 global tariff for 150 days to 24 July 2026 and Section 301 tariffs of 10-12.5% on 60 countries thereafter, leaving the average effective rate at 12.1% in July 2026 versus about 27% in April 2025. Import-heavy hardware and Apple benefited; Section 232 metal and chip tariffs were untouched.

events.title: Gold miners fall 21% in Q2 2026, then recover as gold retakes $4,400
events.summary: After the March war spike, gold slipped below $4,700 in April and posted its worst quarter in 13 years as the 10-year yield climbed about a point from its February low toward 4.7%; GDX fell about 21% from roughly $96 in early April to $75 by 30 June 2026. Gold moved back above $4,400 on 11 August, GDX hit a decade high near $88 (+53% over 12 months) and Newmont reported record Q2 free cash flow of $2.2 billion at a realized price of $4,414 an ounce; gold then fell to a two-month low in October on Fed-hike signals.
events.evidence: GDX about -21% in Q2 2026 (about $96 to $75); gold above $4,400 on 2026-08-11; Newmont Q2 2026 realized gold price $4,414/oz and record $2.2 billion free cash flow.

events.title: Section 232 metals tariffs restructured on full value: 50% metal, 25% derivatives
events.summary: A 2 April 2026 proclamation (effective 6 April) assessed steel, aluminum and copper tariffs on full customs value: 50% on articles made almost entirely of the metals, 25% on derivative products, 15% on certain industrial and grid equipment through 2027, 10% on goods made with US metal, and an exemption for products with 15% or less metal content. The change narrowed the tariff base after the Supreme Court ruling while preserving protection for domestic steel, aluminum and copper producers.
events.evidence: Proclamation signed 2026-04-02: 50% on metal articles, 25% on derivatives, 15% on grid and industrial equipment through 2027, exemption below 15% metal content.

The software ETF IGV bottomed around 13 April 2026, the low from which it rallied 41% into October.

events.title: Software rebounds 41% from the April 'SaaS-pocalypse' low
events.summary: IGV rose 41.46% from 13 April to 12 October 2026, closing at $111.31, as incumbents demonstrated AI upsell within existing contracts, takeover interest resurfaced (PayPal drew Stripe/Advent interest; Figma and others were targets) and vendors shifted toward consumption pricing; the ETF was nonetheless still down 0.68% over one year and up only 5.3% year-to-date, with QQQ +20.8% over the same six months. Analysts characterised the rally as multiple expansion rather than earnings acceleration, leaving it exposed to the October-November tech selloff.

events.title: X-energy's $1 billion IPO and Westinghouse's S-1: nuclear goes public
events.summary: X-energy listed on Nasdaq on 24 April 2026 raising over $1 billion, the largest nuclear IPO on record, weeks after the NRC's first Category II fuel-facility licence for its TX-1 plant; Westinghouse confidentially filed for an IPO on 31 July 2026, and Oklo's Groves test reactor reached criticality on 5 August. The listings monetised the 2024-2025 re-rating and supplied the public market with pure-play SMR and large-reactor equity for the first time.
events.evidence: X-energy Nasdaq IPO on 2026-04-24 raising more than $1 billion; Westinghouse draft S-1 submitted 2026-07-31.

events.title: Commerce orders tool shipments to Hua Hong halted
events.summary: On 28 April 2026 the Commerce Department ordered Applied Materials, Lam Research and KLA to halt certain tool shipments to Hua Hong, China's second-largest foundry, and its Huali subsidiary; the shares were already down 5-6% that day on an OpenAI-related report and came under further pressure. With Lam drawing roughly 35% of recent quarterly revenue from China, the order revived the China-exposure discount on equipment makers at the peak of their 2026 rally.
events.evidence: Commerce halt order on Hua Hong tool shipments reported 2026-04-28; Lam Research about 35% of recent quarterly revenue from China.

events.title: Accenture's worst day on record: -18% on guidance cut and AI fears
events.summary: Accenture reported fiscal Q3 2026 revenue of $18.7 billion (+6%, slightly below consensus), cut full-year growth guidance to 3-4% from 3-5%, disclosed a 2% fall in bookings and about $100 million of Middle East war revenue loss; the stock fell about 18% on 18 June 2026, its worst day ever, with Cognizant -10% to a 52-week low, EPAM -9% (down two-thirds from its January high and dropped from the S&P 500), Capgemini -8.4% and IBM -5%. Investors priced AI coding and agent tools as a structural threat to billable-hour models, leaving Accenture at about 10x earnings.

events.title: Dish DBS, Sling and Boost file for Chapter 11; Hughes follows
events.summary: EchoStar said on 29 June 2026 that Dish DBS, Sling TV and Boost Mobile would file for Chapter 11 by 30 June, citing debt, subscriber losses and spectrum obligations, and Hughes Network Systems filed on 2 August 2026 after a debt maturity; the $23 billion AT&T spectrum sale closed on 28 July. The bankruptcies closed out the satellite pay-TV era and confirmed the three-carrier structure in US wireless.
events.evidence: EchoStar announced the Dish DBS/Sling/Boost Chapter 11 filing on 2026-06-29; AT&T spectrum purchase completed 2026-07-28.

events.title: Semis reverse: Micron -11%, SOX falls as much as 29% from its June peak
events.summary: On 1 July 2026 a report that Meta might rent out excess compute raised fears that AI processing supply was catching up with demand: Micron fell 11% (about $138 billion), Intel 9%, AMD 7%, SMH more than 5%, and Lam, KLA and Applied Materials at least 10%, while Meta rose 9%. Broadcom's AI-revenue guidance of about $16 billion versus $17.2 billion expected, Brent above $84 on Hormuz tensions and reports of a Chinese DUV lithography tool and CXMT's oversubscribed listing extended the drawdown to as much as 29% before a double-digit rebound in early August.

events.title: Data-center backlash: New York's one-year moratorium and a wave of state restrictions
events.summary: Governor Hochul's 14 July 2026 executive order suspended permits for data centers of 50 MW or more for a year; Chicago's mayor called for a moratorium on 11 August, Pennsylvania imposed GRID requirements on 18 August and New Jersey mandated water and power reporting on 27 August, with at least 47 large projects delayed or denied in 2026 and Gallup finding 71% of Americans opposed to local data centers. Rising electricity bills turned the AI-power trade political: utilities were up only 3.5% year-to-date by 5 November 2026 and Goldman estimated moratoria could affect 45% of planned US capacity after the midterms.
events.evidence: New York executive order of 2026-07-14 suspending large data-center construction for one year; XLU +3.5% year-to-date as of 2026-11-05.

events.title: Alphabet falls 7% as 2026 capex rises to $205 billion and cash flow turns negative
events.summary: Alphabet's Q2 2026 report on 22 July raised the top of its 2026 capex range to $205 billion and showed Google Cloud growing 82%, but the company turned cash-flow negative for the first time and its long-term debt had risen 111% to $98 billion in six months; the shares fell 7% on 23 July and Amazon, Meta and Microsoft fell in sympathy ahead of their own reports (Microsoft guiding about $190 billion including finance leases, Amazon about $200-207 billion, Meta up to $145 billion). 'AI fatigue' and debt-funded build-outs became the market's framing for the rest of 2026.

events.title: Fed hikes to 3.75-4% under Warsh, the first increase since July 2023
events.summary: With inflation 'elevated' (2026 headline PCE projected at 3.7%) after the Iran-war energy shock and lingering tariff effects, the FOMC under Chair Kevin Warsh (sworn in 22 May 2026) raised rates 25 bp to 3.75-4% on 16 September 2026 by a 12-0 vote and held on 28 October with two dissents for a further hike; futures priced another increase in December. Higher short rates help bank margins but the 'recent rise in longer-term borrowing costs' and AI-credit stress kept financials (XLF +6.3% year-to-date on 5 November) well behind energy and health care.
events.evidence: FOMC raised the target range to 3.75-4% on 2026-09-16 (12-0), the first hike since July 2023; held 10-2 on 2026-10-28.

events.title: Accenture jumps 22% on fiscal 2027 guidance; IT services snap back
events.summary: On 1 October 2026 Accenture guided fiscal 2027 revenue growth of 3-6% (midpoint above the 3.9% consensus) with Q4 bookings up 4% to $22.17 billion; the shares surged 22%, on track for their best day ever, lifting Cognizant about 8%, Infosys and Wipro 6-7% and IBM 3%. The move reversed part of the June derating and reframed AI as a services tailwind (systems integration, data work) rather than purely a substitution risk, although the group still trades at single-digit to low-teens multiples.
events.evidence: Accenture +22% on 2026-10-01 after guiding FY2027 revenue growth of 3-6%; Q4 bookings $22.17 billion (+4%).

events.title: AI credit stress: CoreWeave bonds distressed, CDS above 1,000 bp, hyperscaler spreads at 2021 highs
events.summary: CoreWeave fell 15.5% on 14 October 2026 as its 2032 bonds dropped to 78 cents (yield 14.8%), 34% between 6 and 21 October and to a record low of $49.92 on 2 November (-44% for the month); its five-year CDS passed 1,000 bp (1,087.8 on 30 October, above 1,289 on 5 November), implying more than 60% five-year default probability on $72 billion of debt, while Oracle's CDS reached about 296-322 bp versus 144 at the start of 2026 and hyperscaler CDS hit their highest since 2021. Gartner (14 October) estimated more than $4 trillion of data-center asset value at write-down risk and BofA (16 October) called AI a classic capital cycle; hyperscalers issued $296 billion of debt in 2026 and reported negative free cash flow in Q3, and OpenAI pushed its IPO to 2027.
